records.quote:
this castaway, that, like a man transplanted into
another planet, was separated by an immense space from his past and
by an immense ignorance from his future.
records.paraphrase: The narrator likens the castaway's alienation among the villagers to a man transplanted to another planet.

records.quote:
His intelligence
is of a scientific order, of an investigating habit, and of that
unappeasable curiosity which believes that there is a particle of a
general truth in every mystery.
records.paraphrase: Kennedy is characterized as possessing a scientific, investigative mind that seeks truth in every mystery.

records.quote:
The Hamburg ship, filling all at once, capsized as she sank, and at daylight
there was not even the end of a spar to be seen above water.
records.paraphrase: The ship capsized and sank completely, leaving no trace above water, with drowned bodies washing ashore.

records.quote:
There was a roof over him, which
seemed made of glass, and was so high that the tallest mountain-pine
he had ever seen would have had room to grow under it. Steam-machines
rolled in at one end and out at the other.
records.paraphrase: A railway station is described through the uncomprehending eyes of the mountaineer, who lacks words for trains and glass roofs.

records.quote:
It was as if these had been the
faces of people from the other world--dead people--he used to tell me
years afterwards. Upon my word, I wonder he did not go mad.
records.paraphrase: The castaway experienced overwhelming loneliness, perceiving the villagers as faces of dead people from another world.

records.quote:
the vessel sunk the night before in Eastbay was the Hamburg emigrant-ship
_Herzogin Sophia-Dorothea_, of appalling memory.
records.paraphrase: The emigrant ship carrying the castaway sank in Eastbay, a notorious disaster.

records.quote:
he told me himself that
he put his trust in God, believing he was no longer in this world. And
truly--he would add--how was he to know?
records.paraphrase: The castaway believed he was no longer alive in the ordinary world after being washed ashore.

records.quote:
the father, cast out mysteriously by
the sea to perish in the supreme disaster of loneliness and despair.
records.paraphrase: The narrator frames the castaway's death as the ultimate consequence of his utter loneliness and estrangement.

records.quote:
At all events, the next time I saw
him he was ill--lung trouble. He was tough, but I daresay he was not
acclimatised as well as I had supposed.
records.paraphrase: Kennedy offers a medical explanation for the stranger's illness, attributing it to lung trouble and failure to acclimatise.

records.quote:
She jumped to her feet, snatched up the child, and stood still. He
spoke to her, and his passionate remonstrances only increased her
fear of that strange man.
records.paraphrase: The mutual incomprehension drives Amy to flee in fear from her dying husband, leaving him helpless.

records.quote:
He gave me to understand
that he had on his passage beheld uncounted multitudes of people--whole
nations--all dressed in such clothes as the rich wear.
records.paraphrase: The mountaineer perceives ordinary travelers as vast multitudes dressed like the rich, contrasting his rural frame of reference with modern industrial society.

records.quote:
the terror, the unreasonable terror, of that man she
could not understand creeping over her.
records.paraphrase: Amy is overcome by an unreasonable terror of the husband she cannot understand as he lies feverish.

records.quote:
Smith, alone amongst his stacks with this apparition, in
the stormy twilight ringing with the infuriated barking of the dog, felt
the dread of an inexplicable strangeness.
records.paraphrase: Smith reacts with dread and takes the stranger for an escaped lunatic upon their inexplicable encounter.

records.quote:
he was a castaway. A poor emigrant from Central Europe bound to
America and washed ashore here in a storm. And for him, who knew nothing
of the earth, England was an undiscovered country.
records.paraphrase: A shipwrecked emigrant is cast onto an English shore that is entirely foreign to him, an undiscovered country.

criteria.rationale: Kennedy is described as having a scientific mind and offers a lay medical remark about lung trouble and failure to acclimatise, but no scientific fact, theory, discovery, natural process, or speculative science is materially represented. These are characterization and ordinary clinical description, not science functioning in the story.

Trains, glass-roofed stations, steamships, and telegraphs appear only as ordinary period technology seen through a bewildered emigrant's eyes. No device or invention speculatively affects the setting, problem, or outcome; these are mundane, contemporary-to-the-story artifacts.

The 'undiscovered country' and 'another planet' phrasings are metaphors for cultural dislocation in a contemporary realist setting. There is no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement.

The story develops consequences of human incomprehension and estrangement, but this is literary tragedy from an interpersonal premise, not extrapolation from an identifiable scientific, technological, or systematic social/historical premise in the science-fiction sense.

Kennedy makes ordinary diagnostic inferences and is called investigative, but no observation, hypothesis, testing, measurement, or evidential revision materially drives understanding or the action. His curiosity is characterization, not demonstrated scientific method.

References to 'another planet,' 'the other world,' and 'undiscovered country' are figurative descriptions of a foreign shore and cultural alienation. There is no actual other planet, dimension, nonordinary cosmic environment, or visitor from one.

The wreck of the emigrant-ship Herzogin Sophia-Dorothea is a large-scale maritime disaster with mass drowning and bodies washing ashore; it is causally central because Yanko is its sole survivor and the entire narrative proceeds from it. This is a technological/human-caused catastrophe rather than a mere personal misfortune.

candidates.description: The shipwrecked Carpathian mountaineer Yanko Goorall, washed ashore in rural England, whose total estrangement from an incomprehensible surrounding society organizes the story. This is a candidate for a novum framed around radical cultural/perceptual displacement, but it is not a world-altering difference from empirical reality.

novelty.rationale: The displacement is cultural and psychological, not a totalizing world-altering difference from the authorial empirical norm. A Central European emigrant shipwrecked on an English coast is entirely consistent with the ordinary historical world; the 'another planet' comparison is an explicit simile, not an ontological change to the story universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The narration supplies a coherent, non-supernatural, immanent account: a scientifically minded doctor reconstructs the man's origin, illness, and death through medical and social reasoning. The logic of estrangement is systematically and rationally developed.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The castaway's incomprehensible strangeness governs the whole narrative logic, driving Amy's terror, her flight, and his death from loneliness and despair. It is the central organizing force of the story rather than an incidental device.

estrangement.rationale: The story renders familiar English industrial society (railway stations, glass roofs, crowds) strange through the uncomprehending eyes of the mountaineer, and renders the mountaineer himself strange to the villagers. This mutual estrangement is powerful literary defamiliarization, but it operates within the ordinary empirical world rather than through a world-altering novum.

candidates.description: The industrial transport apparatus (railways, steam-machines, glass-roofed stations, emigrant steamships) perceived as alien through the mountaineer's frame of reference.

novelty.rationale: Railways, steamships, and stations are ordinary features of the contemporary empirical world, presented as strange only through a naive focalizer. They are not novelties introducing any difference from the author's empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The technology is described coherently and non-supernaturally, consistent with real nineteenth-century industry.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: These industrial scenes are incidental descriptive passages within the man's journey; they do not determine the overriding narrative logic, which concerns his estrangement and death.

estrangement.rationale: The familiar industrial world is defamiliarized through the mountaineer's lack of vocabulary for trains and glass roofs, but this is a rhetorical effect on a real-world referent, not a cognitively estranging novum.
